content.brief:
For Herbie Hancock, the UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador and Chairman of the Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz, inspiring young people to learn about math and science through music has been a life-long dream. For him, there is a profound connection across the disciplines and a way to ignite passion for challenging concepts through music. This was the foundation of the project of Math, Science and Music.

The Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz launched Math, Science & Music in partnership with the U.S. Department of Education as an initiative that uses music as a tool to teach math and science to young people in public and private schools around the world. The program addresses the growing need for students to gain skills and acquire knowledge in science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) subjects and learn to think creatively. The Institute is collaborating with math, science, music and education experts at leading universities and in the private sector to develop a wealth of free engaging curricula, games, apps and other interactive online components.

Studies show that the most crucial years to engage students in STEM learning are grades 4-8. If students begin STEM studies in these early years, they are more likely to continue on this path. Based on this premise, the primary target audience for Math, Science & Music is grades 4-8. The site also offers supplemental curricula that prepare students in grades K-3 for future immersion into the Math Science & Music program, as well as other STEM studies, and supplemental materials for high school and college students to provide them with sequential learning. The Math, Science & Music web site serves as an exciting and engaging repository of free, interactive tools for learning STEM subjects through music, with the aim of preparing students for a world in which technological skills are a necessary and essential part of life.

Curricula in Development

Renowned STEM, music and education experts affiliated with Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), University of California Berkeley, University of Massachusetts, New York University, San Francisco State University, and Johns Hopkins University have all created innovative curricula for Math, Science & Music.

Jeanne Bamberger of MIT and UC Berkeley, Eric Rosenbaum of MIT, and Gena Greher of the University of Massachusetts have developed Making Music Count. This interactive curriculum for grades 4-6 helps teachers engage and develop students’ knowledge of music and its inherent mathematics. The team’s computer music program, Impromptu, helps students understand the concepts of proportion, ratio and common multiples by actually hearing the math happening through music. Students listen to music from their own and others’ cultures to identify the different beats, and create their own beats with the software’s Drumblocks feature.

Eric Rosenbaum at MIT created Scratch Day of Jazz: An International Celebration of Music and Code for students of all ages. The curriculum is based on Scratch, the MIT Media Lab’s free computer programming language especially designed for 8- to 16-year-olds. Scratch Day of Jazz components include the Scratch Design Studio, a two-week online open collaborative activity that includes a gallery of projects created by kids; the Scratch Jazz Celebration on International Jazz Day; a Scratch Jazz web page on the MIT Scratch web site; a Scratch Jazz media collection of audio clips, music loops, images and animation that students can use in their interactive projects; and Makey Makey Jazz Fusion, an activity that will allow students to create their own physical musical instruments that control digital sounds in Scratch.

New York University music education professor Alex Ruthmann developed Groove Pizza: An Interface for Music and Geometry for elementary school students. By placing rhythms on a circular timeline, the Groove Pizza will show metrical function and relationships that may not be evident in standard music notation. Seeing shapes and patterns on the timeline will make it easier for students to understand them aurally. Groove Pizza also supports the playful learning of mathematical and scientific concepts, including ratios, angles, symmetry, and the placement of electrons in atomic orbitals. Also from Dr. Ruthmann is aQWERTYon: An Exploration in Improvisation for students of all ages. This accordion uses the Q, W, E, R, T and Y keys on a standard computer keyboard to simplify the process for students to improvise, make music, and play along with their favorite YouTube videos.

Sue Courey and Endre Balogh of San Francisco State University are creating Addressing the Algebra Blues with Jazz, with a Fractions and Rhythm curriculum for elementary school students, Proportional Reasoning and DJ Mixing for middle school students, and Algebra and Jazz for high school students. The fractions lesson plans will incorporate the Kodaly music education approach, which promotes experiential learning. The proportional reasoning curriculum will introduce students to the song mixing process and teach them to calculate a song’s beats per minute. The algebra lesson plans will focus on jazz history, rhythms and notation, and the music’s connection to formal algebra concepts and symbols. All three curricula will introduce difficult mathematical concepts in engaging ways through music. Students will learn the relationship of musical rhythms to numbers; read musical notes and perform rhythmic patterns by clapping and drumming; and work toward adding musical notes, identifying rhythms, and creating their own pieces.

At Harvard University, pianist, composer and scholar Vijay Iyer has overseen the development of The Mathematical Foundations of Indian Rhythm, for elementary school students. This program demonstrates ways of visualizing rhythms using mathematical proportions, employing symmetric musical shapes, and calculating musical combinations and possibilities. The lessons are useful for students working on a variety of skills: basic arithmetic, fractions and ratios, geometry, algebra, and permutations and combinations. In addition, Professor Iyer has created the Cognition and Improvisation video lecture series for college students. Neuroscience and neurophysics scholars will demonstrate how we hear sounds and music, what our brains do with auditory information, and the ways in which this informs how we function as humans individually and in a group.

Daniel Naiman of Johns Hopkins University has contributed The Mathematics of Music. This college curriculum explores through a mathematical framework questions that arise in our understanding of sound and music, such as: What is harmony? What does it mean to tune an instrument? What is it that gives a musical instrument its particular characteristic sound? How can sounds be modified to achieve various effects? When a musician improvises, how can we model the effect of spontaneity?

The Institute plans to continue expanding the Math, Science & Music curricula for students in grades 4-6. Current plans prioritize the addition of more middle school curricula, including for 7th and 8th grades, plus 9th grade high school curricula in the years to come. These new Math, Science & Music lesson plans will be accompanied by a growing number of play-based games, apps and video interfaces that will reach a wider audience. New partnerships will be established with additional researchers and scholars whose lesson plans will complement and expand upon the existing curricula.

The Institute also plans to deepen its experience-based work by conducting further field testing and pilot groups in Boston and San Francisco, as well as Washington, D.C. and other school districts. These urban districts serve diverse student populations, including a significant number of African-American and Hispanic/Latino students, and students from low- and moderate-income families.

Math, Science & Music will be promoted widely and integrated into public schools across the United States through partnerships with the U.S. Department of Education, State Superintendents of Education, and other education leaders. The Institute is also in discussion with UNESCO, the United Nations agency devoted to education and science, to disseminate the curriculum internationally.

Key Contributors

S. Alex Ruthmann, PhD

S. Alex Ruthmann, PhD, Director of the NYU Music Experience Design Lab, is a researcher, educator and musician whose research and practice explores new media musicianship, creative computing, the creative processes of young musical creators, and the development of music and media technologies for use in school- and community-based youth programs. He and his collaborators are the recipients of two National Science Foundation grants exploring the interdisciplinary teaching of computational and musical thinking. Dr. Ruthmann is President of the Association for Technology in Music Instruction, Past Chair of the Creativity special research interest group of the Society for Research in Music Education, and Co-Editor of the International Journal of Education & the Arts. Dr. Ruthmann received an interdisciplinary B.Mus. degree from the University of Michigan in Music and Technology, and M.Mus. and Ph.D. degrees in Music Education from Oakland University.

Eric Rosenbaum, PhD

Eric Rosenbaum’s work explores the intersection of music, play and improvisation. Dr. Rosenbaum’s projects include the hugely popular Makey Makey invention kit, as well as software for finger painting with sound, painting with light, improvising with looping sounds, and creating interactive behaviors in 3D virtual worlds. His speaking appearances have included TEDx Pioneer Valley, Economist Tech Frontiers, and Dust or Magic App Camp. Dr. Rosenbaum’s work has been featured at the San Francisco Exploratorium, Smithsonian National Museum of American History, San Jose Tech Museum, and OFFFmatica and CineKid festivals. He received a bachelor’s degree in psychology and a master’s degree in technology in education from Harvard University. Dr. Rosenbaum also holds a master’s degree in media arts and sciences from MIT Media Lab, for which he developed Jots, a system to support reflective learning in the Scratch programming environment. Rosenbaum completed his PhD in the Lifelong Kindergarten group at MIT Media Lab.

Jeanne Bamberger

A highly respected pioneer in musical development and cognition, Jeanne Bamberger is Professor Emerita of Music and Urban Education at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Adjunct Professor of Music at the University of California, Berkeley, where she teaches music theory and music cognition. Her interests include musical development and learning, in particular aspects of representations among both children and adults. She was a student of Artur Schnabel and Roger Sessions, and has performed extensively as piano soloist and in chamber music ensembles. Bamberger attended Columbia University and the University of California at Berkeley, receiving degrees in philosophy and music theory. Her recent books include The Mind Behind the Musical Ear (Harvard University Press), Developing Musical Intuitions: A Project Based Introduction to Making and Understanding Music (Oxford University Press), and Discovering the Musical Mind: A View of Creativity as Learning (Oxford University Press).

Gena Greher

Gena Greher is Professor and Coordinator of Music Education at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. She teaches undergraduate and graduate level music classes in music methods, popular culture, and technology applications in music education as well as an interdisciplinary course in computing and music. Dr. Greher has published on the influence of integrating multimedia technology into the general music classroom, the middle school music curriculum and the music teacher education curriculum. She is the co-author with Jesse Heines of Computational Thinking in Sound: Teaching the Art and Science of Music and Technology. A graduate of New York’s High School of Performing Arts, Dr. Greher earned a bachlelor’s degree in violin performance at Queens College and a master’s degree in broadcasting and film from Boston University. She received her EdM and EdD from Teachers College Columbia University, where she was the Project Associate for the Creative Arts Laboratory, a professional development proram in arts education. Before receiving her Doctorate in Music Education, Dr. Greher spent 20 years as an award-winning jingle producer and music director for multinational advertising agencies.

Vijay Iyer

Vijay Iyer is a GRAMMY nominated jazz pianist and composer who in 2014 began a permanent appointment as Rosenblatt Professor of the Arts at Harvard University’s Department of Music. According to The New York Times, “There’s probably no frame wide enough to encompass the creative output of the pianist Vijay Iyer.” DownBeat Magazine’s 2015 Artist of the Year, Iyer is also a 2013 MacArthur Fellow and a 2012 Doris Duke Performing Artist. Other honors include the Greenfield Prize, the Alpert Award in the Arts, and the New York Foundation for the Arts Fellowship. Iyer has a bachelor’s degree in mathematics and physics from Yale University, and received an interdisciplinary PhD in the cognitive science of music from the University of California Berkeley. He has published in Journal of Consciousness Studies, Wire, Music Perception, JazzTimes, Journal of the Society for American Music, Critical Studies in Improvisation, Sound Unbound, and The Best Writing in Mathematics: 2010.

Daniel Naiman

Daniel Naiman graduated with a B.A. in Mathematics summa cum laude from Cornell University and went on to earn a master’s degree in Statistics and a PhD in Mathematics from University of Illinois Urbana/Champaign. He joined the Applied Mathematics and Statistics faculty of Johns Hopkins University, where he has risen to Full Professor and served as Department Chair from 2004 to 2014. At Johns Hopkins, Naiman has taught courses in algebra, probability, statistics, stochastic processes and computing. While pursuing his interests in mathematics, Dr. Naiman has maintained a strong commitment to musical study, appreciation and performance. An alto and tenor saxophonist, he has played in five different big bands over the past 40 years. More recently, he has taken up the electric bass and baritone saxophone, and performed with small jazz groups.

Sue Courey

Sue Courey is currently the Department Chair of Early Childhood General and Special Education at the Touro Graduate School of Education in New York City. Prior to joining the Touro Graduate School of Education in May 2016, Dr. Courey was an Associate Professor of Special Education and the Mild/Moderate Program Coordinator in the Department of Special Education at San Francisco State University. Recently awarded Professor Emerita at San Francisco State University, Dr. Courey continues work with colleagues and doctoral students on research projects in the areas of mathematics and learning challenges, mathematics and music, teacher preparation, and Universal Design for Learning. She received her PhD in special education, high incidence disabilities at Vanderbilt University. Dr. Courey’s research interests include teaching mathematics to students with learning differences.

Web Site Developer 

NYU Music Experience Design Lab (MusEDLab)

The New York University MusEDLab is leading the team creating the comprehensive educational platform for Math, Science & Music. The NYU Music Experience Design Lab is one of the nation’s most respected developers of online music creativity and learning tools. Dr. Ruthmann and his team work with the Institute’s university partners to develop games, apps, and video interfaces that are aligned with the lesson plan content. All of these interactive elements are then integrated into the Math, Science & Music educational website. The interactive elements being created by Dr. Ruthmann and his team help make the lessons accessible and relevant to students and their teachers and parents.

content.brief: The EcoSonic (Ecology/Sound) Playground Project inspires children to design, build, and play large­scale, social, musical instruments. Children collect and then work with reusable materials to create original instruments, use architectural plans to build scaffolding, and then attach their instruments to this scaffolding to make one inclusive instrument (these tend to be 5 foot cubes or bigger). Each EcoSonic Playground Project comes with structural and standards‐based STEAM integrated curriculum materials to guide the making‐to‐playing process. The project is adaptable to all ages, learning styles, and types of spaces.

Music Cognition: The Biological Foundations of Music

How does it relate to us as human beings? And how do we make sense of it?

content.brief:
Our goal is to provide a working environment where students can play with, make explicit and develop the powerful musical know-how and its implicit mathematics that they enjoy everyday in making sense of the music all around them.

 Just “keeping time” as we listen to music is a critical beginning, Following the beat surprisingly becomes a path into the mathematics that strongly helps to organize musical time. Working with our interactive computer music program, Impromptu, proportional numbers representing time values become a compositional medium for joining music and math, where students are actually hearing the math happening.

content.brief:
Music is the pleasure the human mind experiences from counting without being aware that it is counting.

Implicit in this statement is the notion that all of us who appreciate music must, on at least a subconscious level, be appreciating its mathematical structure. It seems plausible therefore that one ought to be able use musical appreciation to motivate attaining better understanding of related mathematics. The purpose of a course in the Mathematics of Music is to expose students who appreciate music to mathematical ideas.

The aim of the pages linked to here, is to, by way of instruction, present to the reader some examples of connections between music and mathematics, and hence a sense for the flavor of the Mathematics of Music course.

content.brief:
The Mathematical Foundations of Indian Rhythm

This series of lessons will help students learn math using visualizations and hands-on exercises based on the Karnatic rhythmic system of South India. Karnatik music involves a deep, embodied understanding of mathematical proportions, symmetry, and linear rhythmic combinations. Through exposure to these creative methods, students will gain a richer understanding of the aesthetics of mathematical principles and use multiple learning modalities to visualize, hear, and feel musical proportions, combinations, and relationships. The lessons also provide a kind of cultural immersion that helps to bolster students' understanding of how math and music are interconnected around the world.

content.brief: Academic Music utilizes authentic music instruction to explore various math concepts. This program encourages deeper learning and provides the opportunity to reach students from every level of ability, ethnicity, and linguistic background. While music concepts and theory align with all areas of the mathematics curriculum, we focus on aligning concepts of rhythm with basic fraction concepts at the elementary level. In middle school, we align basic Jazz concepts and octaves with proportional reasoning. Both programs address the lack of engaging curriculum and teaching methodologies that support understanding of difficult math concepts at the elementary and middle school level.

content.brief:
OIID is a unique interactive interface that allows the listener to step inside music and interact with music in an unprecedented way.

The platform allows the listener to 'deconstruct' a song down to its separate tracks/instruments for a unique individual remix - creating a new dimension to the music experience.

The OIID interface in MathScienceMusic can help students engage with mathematical problems such as fraction, geometry and algebra.

Chrome Music Lab is a website that makes learning music more accessible through fun, hands-on experiments. Many teachers have been using Chrome Music Lab as a tool in their classrooms to explore music and its connections to science, math, art, and more. They’ve been combining it with dance and live instruments. Here’s a collection of some uses found on Twitter.
